rendered:
The paper gives no amount for nickel, manganese or cobalt leaching. It says they did not leach at all: the Ni, Mn and Co ratios in the NMC622 stayed consistent before and after the separation process[1], which the authors read as showing that the process does not leach those transition metals[2]. They cite ICP-OES results as confirming this, but those results are in Table S1 of the supplement, which is not part of this document. The only leaching the paper reports is of lithium, which it says occurred after recovery.

On the ether question, the paper does not blame the ether groups for transition-metal loss. It attributes lithium loss to them: The Cyrene molecule has two ether groups,[3] and which will attract lithium cation because ether is electron-donating,[4] so the ether groups draw lithium ions out of the cathode, resulting in lithium leaching and causing the high-Ni cathode more[5] unstable. The paper also links the electrochemical degradation of the recovered NMC622 to lithium leaching together with possible surface changes caused by the Cyrene solvent.
